To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stable acetaldehyde adduction of lysine residues in peptides derived from the amine terminal beta-globin peptide of human hemoglobin has been demonstrated.
stable adducts of hemoglobin with acetaldehyde have a Schiff base structure and that the epsilon-amino groups and the amino terminus of hemoglobin are potential targets of acetaldehyde.
acetaldehyde adduction to the amine termini of peptides is possible and stable, and that acetaldehyde can form stable Schiff base adduction to lysine sidechains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural characterization of stable Schiff bases formed between acetaldehyde and proteins.
the structural characterization of acetic acid, acetaldehyde, and acetone adducts of proteins and peptides.
the characterization of acetaldehye adducts of hemoglobin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the N-terminal Val and the epsilon-amino group of lysine in hemoglobin beta-globin are potential targets for acetaldehyde.
acetaldehyde reacts with the N-terminal amide group of Val as a stable Schiff base, and with the epsilon-amino group of Lys as a stable Schiff-base adduct.
acetaldehyde adduction of hemoglobin is a complex process and that the adducts that are formed depend on many factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acetaldehyde reacts with both the N-terminal amide and the epsilon-amino group of lysine residues of the N-terminal beta-globein chain peptides of hemoglobin.
acetaldehyde adduction of proteins can occur in vivo and in vitro.
the epsilon-amino groups on the lysine residues are more susceptible to acetaldehyde modification than the N-terminal amide groups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
acetaldehyde can be a reactive metabolite of ethanol in vivo, and that stable Schiff bases of hemoglobin can be formed.
acetaldehyde adduction of the epsilon-amino group of lysine residues is possible.
the amine termini of hemoglobin and other proteins may also be targets for stable acetaldehyde adduction.
